name: Mushroom diet (M-plan)

card.summary: A two-week plan that replaces one meal a day with a mushroom dish, promoted for leaning the body and supporting a slimmer physique.
card.note: Dietitians quoted in press describe it as a low-calorie diet and say spot slimming cannot be targeted.

quick.overview:
The M-plan is a fad diet in which one meal a day, usually lunch or dinner, is replaced with a mushroom-based dish for about 14 days. It was promoted around 2013 with claims of slimming the hips, waist and thighs.

Dietitians quoted in the press describe it as a low-calorie diet, and note that fat loss cannot be directed to a body area. Separate research on mushrooms in the diet includes a one-year trial of substituting mushrooms for meat, which reported effects on body weight and composition.
quick.how: Participants swap a single meal each day for a mushroom dish, such as a mushroom-based soup, stir-fry or burger, and eat normally otherwise.
quick.risks: A plan built on a single food is described by commentators as unrealistic if it dropped calories too far. Mushroom-only eating would not supply enough calories, and some people avoid raw mushrooms or have allergies.

lead: The mushroom diet, known as the M-plan, is a fad diet in which one meal a day is replaced with mushrooms for two weeks.[1] It was marketed on the promise of slimming the hips, waist and thighs, and press coverage around 2013 linked it to celebrities such as Katy Perry and Kelly Osbourne.[2]

People use it as a short fat-loss routine to get a leaner look. Dietitians quoted in coverage called it simply a low-calorie diet and said no diet can promise weight loss from a chosen area.[2] Wikipedia notes that reported benefits of mushrooms come largely from observational research.[1]

chain: Mushroom dish replaces one daily meal
Lower body fat for a leaner look
angle.text: The plan works through swapping a meal for a low-calorie mushroom dish for two weeks, aiming at a slimmer midsection and limbs. It is a short-term fat-loss routine rather than a targeted body change.

infobox: One meal a day replaced with mushrooms

paras: The M-plan substitutes a mushroom meal for lunch or dinner for two weeks.[1][2] One outlet reported that the plan has no book, website or identified origin.[2]

Dietitians said the diet amounts to calorie reduction and that spot reduction is not possible.[2] McGill's Dr. Joseph Schwarcz has argued that many mushroom health studies have flaws, such as not accounting for the rest of the diet.[1]

A one-year randomized trial in Appetite (2013) examined substituting mushrooms for meat and reported on body weight, body composition and health parameters.[3] A 2024 randomized trial found that adding mushrooms to a Mediterranean-style diet did not change most short-term cardiometabolic risk factors.[4] No trial has tested the M-plan itself.

timeline.event: Press coverage links the M-plan to celebrities.[2]
